title: Routine Canopy Work, Plant Condition and Work-Order Boundaries

content.overview: Routine canopy work is controlled plant handling, not an invitation to redesign plant architecture from personal preference. Learners practice confirming the room and work order, inspecting plant condition before beginning, performing only the authorized pruning, defoliation, support, spacing or training task, protecting sanitation between plants and areas, recognizing excessive damage or plant conditions that require a hold, and recording work honestly.

vocabulary.definition: The spatial arrangement of stems, branches, leaves and reproductive sites in a plant canopy.
Canopy shaping that repositions or supports shoots without intentionally causing major tissue damage.
Training that intentionally removes, cuts or substantially damages tissue and therefore requires an appropriate recovery context.
The supplied task-specific definition of what plant work is required, acceptable and complete.

sections.title: Anatomy and developmental stage determine what canopy work means
sections.body: Roots, stems, nodes, internodes, leaves and meristems form one connected transport and growth system. Nodes mark repeated structural units, internodes define spacing, and apical or axillary meristems generate new shoot growth. The same cut or bend can produce different consequences in a small seedling, rapidly expanding vegetative plant, transition plant or flowering crop because resource allocation, tissue maturity and reproductive development are different. Canopy work should therefore be tied to the identified structure and developmental context rather than plant height alone.

sections.title: Inspect before modifying the plant
sections.body: Confirm plant or room identity, developmental context, vigor and any visible damage or pest/disease concern before beginning canopy work. A plant already showing a meaningful abnormality may require a hold or escalation rather than routine cutting or manipulation.

sections.title: The work order controls scope
sections.body: The technician performs the defined pruning, defoliation, support, spacing or training task to the supplied standard. Personal preference for topping, aggressive defoliation or another technique does not override the work order, plant condition or developmental stage.

sections.title: Protect tissue and sanitation
sections.body: Use the supplied handling and sanitation method between plants or zones. Avoid unnecessary tissue damage, contaminated tool movement and support placement that cuts, constricts or abrades stems. When unintended damage occurs, document it rather than hiding it with additional pruning.

sections.title: Evaluate completion against the standard
sections.body: A canopy task is complete when the assigned plants were handled to the defined standard and exceptions were documented. Uniformity should be evaluated from the requested structural outcome and crop condition, not from making every plant visually identical regardless of biology.

workedExamples: A work order calls for selective lower-canopy cleanup. A coworker suggests heavy whole-plant defoliation. The technician follows the work order and escalates any needed change rather than substituting a personal technique.
A branch cracks during repositioning. The technician follows the supplied response, records the plant and damage, and avoids continuing to force the branch merely to match neighboring plants.
commonMistakes: Applying a preferred training method even when it is not the assigned task.
Removing additional tissue to make all plants look identical.
Continuing routine canopy work through fresh pest signs without applying biosecurity/escalation controls.
Hiding accidental plant damage rather than recording the exception.
content.practicalApplication: Execute a simulated canopy-maintenance work order containing a weak plant, a plant with fresh pest-like damage, a support placement risk and one accidental tissue injury. Use the downloadable canopy work-order practice sheet to document task scope, sanitation, quarantine/hold decisions, before/after verification, exceptions and handoff.
content.summary: Technician I canopy work links controlled instructions with plant condition. The technician confirms scope, handles tissue carefully, protects sanitation, stops when plant condition or authorization requires it, and documents actual completion instead of substituting personal technique.

blocks.title: Assigned canopy work versus independent redesign

left.label: Technician I task execution
left.body: Confirm identity and plant condition, follow the defined pruning/support/training standard, protect sanitation and document exceptions.

right.label: Out-of-scope redesign
right.body: Choose a different high-stress technique, remove substantially more tissue or change the production strategy without authorization.

blocks.title: Plant anatomy and developmental growth stages
blocks.alt: Educational cannabis plant diagram identifying roots, stem, nodes, internodes, leaves and growth points alongside seedling, vegetative, transition and flowering developmental stages.
blocks.caption: Identify the structure and stage before acting. Node position, meristem location, tissue maturity and reproductive development all change the biological meaning of canopy work.

blocks.title: Canopy work-order scope and stop boundary
blocks.alt: Canopy decision flow from pre-task inspection to authorized work and result verification, with stop or hold conditions for severe stress, tissue splitting, pest concern, or ambiguous instructions.
blocks.caption: Canopy work is controlled execution. Plant condition and the supplied work standard define when to proceed, stop, hold, clarify or escalate.

blocks.title: Biosecurity and quarantine workflow
blocks.alt: Clean-to-dirty movement diagram showing sanitation checkpoints, suspect plant isolation, quarantine boundaries, breach documentation and escalation.
blocks.caption: Canopy work must not become a contamination or pest-spread pathway. Movement and tool control continue even when the production task is routine.

blocks.title: Pest signs during pruning
blocks.setting: A pruning crew discovers fresh feeding damage and suspicious insects on several plants in one work area.
options: Continue through all rooms with the same tools
Protect the supplied biosecurity boundary, stop or isolate work as required and escalate the finding
Prune off the evidence and discard it without a record
Move the suspect plants through clean rooms for comparison
blocks.answer: Protect the supplied biosecurity boundary, stop or isolate work as required and escalate the finding
blocks.feedback: Canopy work must not become a contamination or pest-spread pathway. The observation and boundary response take priority over routine task completion.
